label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
11 November 2026

Dear Kelechi,

You said put it in writing, so here it is. On paper, with a stamp, through your letterbox in Croydon like a council tax bill. I hope you're reading this on the train like you promised and not at your desk pretending it's a costing.

Let me say what I want first so you can relax. I'm not asking you to resign. I'm not asking you to sign anything. I'm asking you to come to one open evening: Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I'll come with you. If you hate it, you go back to your spreadsheet on Friday morning and I will never mention it again. (I will mention it again. But less.)

Now, why I wasn't joking at my birthday.

You've been at that firm nine years. Every time I see you, you tell me every day is the same spreadsheet, I say "so leave", you laugh, and we order more food. Fine. But on your last birthday you went a bit quiet and said, "I just want to do something that matters before 40." You're 34. I'm not the one who said it o. I'm just the one who remembered.

And here's what I know about you that your firm doesn't care about. You got an A in further maths. You were the one tutoring half of Moremi before exams, and nobody ever left feeling stupid. That last part is the bit you can't train into people. I work with teachers who know the maths inside out and still can't do it. You could do it at 19, with no sleep.

You can still do it, because I watched you at Christmas. My nephew had been fighting fractions for months. You took the jollof, shared it out on plates, and in fifteen minutes he understood something his teacher and his auntie (a qualified maths teacher, thank you) had failed to get into his head. He still talks about it. He asks me when Uncle Kelechi is coming back, and I'm trying not to take it personally.

So that's you. Let me tell you about us.

My school in Peckham has 1,100 kids. Since September, two of our Year 9 maths groups have been covered by a supply teacher. I've got nothing against the person, they're doing their best, but that's two classes of thirteen-year-olds with no proper maths teacher of their own, in the year when a lot of kids decide whether they're "a maths person" or not. We can't find people. Meanwhile somebody who can explain fractions with rice is in Croydon checking other people's costings. Kelechi, you're wasting yourself. I said it at the party and I'm saying it sober.

Last month a boy in my Year 11 class, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations. Three weeks we'd been on it. Three weeks of him looking at me like I was speaking Greek. Then one lesson it just dropped, and he shouted "is that all??" across the room, and the whole class clapped for him. I was smiling for the rest of the day. I don't get that every day, I won't lie. But I get it, and I'd bet money your spreadsheet has never once clapped.

Now the bad parts, because I know you. If I only tell you the sweet side you won't believe any of it.

Teaching is hard. The marking is endless. You finish one pile and another one is waiting, and it follows you home. Behaviour some days is wahala, proper wahala, and there are lessons where you plan something beautiful and it dies in the first five minutes. When I started in 2019 I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. I've never hidden that from you and I'm not going to start now. It got better. By the second year I knew what I was doing, and now most days I actually like going in, which is more than you can say and you know it.

Then the money. The route I'm talking about is the salaried one. You're paid while you train, so you're not going back to being a broke student. It's one year, starting September 2027. Yes, your pay will drop that first year, I'm not going to dress it up. After that it goes up, and there's a proper pension, and the holidays are real. You know I disappear every August. That could be you. Bring your questions about the actual numbers on the 19th, that's exactly what the evening is for, and you of all people know how to interrogate a figure.

And before you start with "I'm too old to be starting again", abeg. A woman in my department started at 41. She's one of the best we have, and the kids don't know or care what she did before. You'd be qualified at 36, and you'd walk in with nine years of real work behind you, which is more than most of us had. When a Year 9 asks "when will I ever use this", you'd be the only person in the building with a decent answer.

I'm not saying it will be easy and I'm not saying it's a calling or any of that. You know I don't talk like that. I'm saying you're patient, you're funny, you can make hard things feel simple, and kids would love you. I've seen a lot of people try this job and I'm telling you, as your friend since Unilag and as somebody who does it every day, that you'd be good at it. Maybe very good. Don't let it enter your head.

Applications for next September open soon, which is why I'm chasing you now and not in the new year when you've talked yourself out of it. So come and look. Listen to them, ask your difficult quantity surveyor questions, eat whatever biscuits they put out. I'll be right next to you. Afterwards we'll go and eat and you can tell me everything that's wrong with the idea.

Thursday 19 November, 6pm, Lewisham. Just send me "yes" and we'll sort out where to meet.

Your friend, whether you like it or not,

P.S. Yes, I really posted it. You said proper letter, not voice note. Next time be careful what you ask for.

P.P.S. If you don't reply I'm sending the next one recorded delivery so you have to sign for it.

I left the space under the sign-off empty so you can sign it by hand after printing.

reasons: The final sentence is a note about the task rather than part of the letter.
